stages.summary: Read your notes on Wren. They are in your journal. Use Look.
Say hello to Wren. Use Talk in the waiting room.

narrative_lines: Wren slides off the chair, tucks Biscuit under one arm, and picks up her sneakers with her free hand. She stays a step behind you, waiting for you to lead the way.
Afternoon light slants across the road rug. Wren goes straight to the two lidded bins at the end of the shelf and starts moving the wooden animals between them. A cow, a pig, a little brown horse.
Wren (to Isla): One, two, three...
She catches herself counting out loud and stops. She puts the cow in the left bin, takes it back out, and sets it in the right one so both bins have the same number.
Wren (to Isla): These ones live in this house, and those ones live in that house.
Once both bins are even, Wren checks them one more time, left and then right, and pats her hands together.
Wren (to Isla): Do you have any of the little oranges today?
Wren (to Isla): And if there's crackers, can mine be cut in squares?
Once both bins are even, Wren checks them one more time, left and then right, and pats her hands together.
Wren (to Isla): Do you have any of the little oranges today?
Wren (to Isla): And if there's crackers, can mine be cut in squares?

stages.summary: Fetch the clementine and crackers from the kitchen and return to Wren in the playroom.

narrative_lines: Wren lines the orange peel up along the edge of the napkin. When the last piece of cracker is gone, she pulls Biscuit's canvas bag onto her lap and unzips it to check what's inside. A small toothbrush, a notebook, and a rolled-up sock with something hard inside it. She packs them back in the exact same order.
Wren (to Isla): I packed Biscuit's toothbrush in here too, just in case we go to the other house.
You take the folded square of oatmeal cloth from your tote and drape it over the toy shelf. Wren watches you do it, then reaches out to tug the left corner down so the hem hangs straight.
Isla (to Wren): Stories first. The toys can rest for a bit.
Wren (to Isla): This side was hanging down a little crooked.
You switch on the warm lamp by the beanbag and turn off the overhead light. Wren climbs onto the mustard cushion, passing the blue one by without looking at it, and settles Biscuit in her lap.
On the first page, a small brown bird sits between two tall trees, clutching a woven twig nest against her chest with both wings.

Isla (to Wren): Once there was a little bird with a very good nest. In the morning she flew to the oak tree, and in the afternoon she flew to the maple tree, and she carried her nest with her the whole way.
Wren leans over the page and traces the curve of the bird's wing with her fingertip.
Wren (to Isla): She's holding onto it the whole time she flies. Her wings must get really tired.

Wren reaches into Biscuit's bag and pulls out the small notebook. She opens it flat on her knee and tilts it toward you. Across the page is a neat row of crayon squares, yellow and green, each marked with a pencil check.
Wren (to Isla): Look, I made a calendar. Yellow is for Mom's house and green is for Dad's apartment. I check it every night before I go to sleep.
You turn the page. In the next picture, a rabbit and a spotted owl sit on a low branch, reaching out to help.
Isla (to Wren): Let me hold that nest for a minute, said Rabbit, so you can rest your wings. No thank you, said Bird, I have to keep it safe. Let me hold it, said Owl. No thank you, said Bird.
Wren looks away from the book and glances toward the open space on the rug.
Wren (to Isla): Hey, Isla, I learned how to do three cartwheels in a row at recess. I won't do one in here because of the lamp.
Before you can read the next line, Wren lifts Biscuit up to her mouth and whispers something right into his chewed ear. Then she lowers him and looks at you.
Wren (to Isla): I told Biscuit a secret. He's the only one I tell, because he doesn't talk.
You turn to the last page. Soft gray rain falls between the two trees, and the little bird is curled on the mossy ground in the middle, her wings tucked in and the nest resting beside her.

Isla (to Wren): That evening the rain came down, and Bird's wings were too tired to fly another inch. So she set her nest down on the soft ground right between the two trees. Both trees stretched their branches over her to keep off the rain, and Bird went to sleep.
Wren stays very still, looking at the picture.
Wren (to Isla): She finally put it down, and neither tree got mad.

For a long moment the only sound is the rain-like hum from the hallway. Then Wren unzips Biscuit's bag, reaches all the way to the bottom, and takes out the rolled-up sock. She unwraps it on her knees. Inside is the curved blue handle of a teacup, broken off in one piece.
Wren (to Isla): Look. The whole handle came off in one piece.
On the first page, a big brown bear stands in a meadow holding a single bright red balloon.
Isla (to Wren): Bear had one red balloon on a string. Then he found two yellow balloons by the fence, and three blue ones by the pond.
Wren sits up a little straighter and taps the balloons with her finger as she counts.
Wren (to Isla): Four, five, six. Look, the sixth one is stuck in the tree.

Wren reaches into Biscuit's bag and pulls out the small notebook. She opens it flat on her knee and tilts it toward you. Across the page is a neat row of crayon squares, yellow and green, each marked with a pencil check.
Wren (to Isla): Look, I made a calendar. Yellow is for Mom's house and green is for Dad's apartment. I check it every night before I go to sleep.
You turn to the last page. All ten balloons float up into a wide evening sky while Bear waves from the hill.
Isla (to Wren): Nine, ten. A breeze came along, and Bear let all ten balloons float up into the sky.
Wren (to Isla): Now he doesn't have any left. Ten is the end of the book.
The cover shows a little red fox standing on a path between two small houses. Wren stares at the cover without moving. As soon as you open to the first page, she puts her hand flat over the words.
Wren (to Isla): I don't want to read this one today.
On the shelf, the little pear-shaped timer gives its soft five-minute warning click. Wren looks over at it, then back at you.
Wren (to Isla): Does that mean our time is almost up?

stages.summary: Sit on the back steps. Go through the kitchen and out the back.
narrative_lines: The timer on the shelf gives its single soft chime. Wren tucks Biscuit into the crook of her arm and stands up. By the door she sets her sneakers down side by side, toes even, and slips her feet into them.
Out in the waiting room, Gloria is already on her feet. Wren's mother is standing just inside the front door with her coat still buttoned.
Mom (to Wren): Hey, baby. Sorry I'm a couple minutes late. Ready to head home?
Wren (to Isla): Bye, Isla. See you next Thursday.
Back in the playroom, she has left a sheet of paper on the low table.
It is a drawing, in crayon. A row of crayons, all the same length, colored in one at a time.
The front door clicks shut behind them, and the house settles into quiet.

The back steps are cold and the late afternoon sky is gray. You set your canvas tote beside you on the top step and sit down for five minutes before heading round to unchain your bike. Inside your tote, your phone has buzzed.

stages.summary: Fetch a picture book from the book room, at the top of the house.
narrative_lines: You reach into your tote bag for a picture book. There is a pencil stub, a tissue and the timer, and no book.
Isla (to Wren): I left the books upstairs. I'll be right back.

stages.summary: Choose a picture book from the book room, at the top of the house.
narrative_lines: Wren (to Isla): Are we doing a story?
Isla (to Wren): We are. I need to pick one first. I'll be right back.

stages.summary: Take the book back to Wren in the playroom.

narrative_lines: You read your note through once, then close the journal. You sit on the top step a little longer, listening to a city bus sigh at the Calloway stop, before heading round to the front porch for your bike.

stages.summary: Read your notes on Leo. They are in your journal. Use Look.
narrative_lines: It is early February, and the front steps are slushy. You chain your bike to the porch rail and unclip your tote.
Through the glass in the green door, a boy in a puffy red coat is standing at the fish tank. He taps the glass once, near the snail, and waits.
Your journal is in your tote, with your notes on him. When you are ready, you can go in and say hello.

stages.summary: Say hello to Leo. Use Talk in the waiting room.

narrative_lines: Leo is out the door before you stand up, one untied lace slapping the floor. In the hall he waits for you with his arms crossed.
Late light comes through the bay window onto the road rug. Leo goes straight to the toy shelf, still in his red coat, and pulls out the doctor's kit.
He hangs the plastic stethoscope around his neck and pushes a sheet of paper and a red crayon into your hands.
Leo (to Isla): You're the chart nurse. Write down everything I say.
You set the basket of stuffed animals on the low table. A one-eyed frog, an owl and a lamb look out over the rim.
Leo (to Isla): First patients. Frog, Owl, Lamb. Nurse, write that down.

stages.summary: Fetch the basket of stuffed animals from the quiet room, on the second floor.
narrative_lines: Late light comes through the bay window onto the road rug. Leo goes straight to the toy shelf, still in his red coat, and pulls out the doctor's kit.
He hangs the plastic stethoscope around his neck and pushes a sheet of paper and a red crayon into your hands.
Leo (to Isla): You're the chart nurse. Write down everything I say.
Leo looks into your empty hands, then at the door.
Leo (to Isla): Nurse! Where are the patients? Go and get them. Quick.
You remember the basket he asked for last week, up in the quiet room.

stages.summary: Take the basket back to Leo in the playroom.

narrative_lines: You set the basket on the low table. A one-eyed frog, an owl and a lamb look out over the rim.
Leo (to Isla): About time, Nurse. First patients. Frog, Owl, Lamb. Write that down.
Leo kneels over the frog and presses the stethoscope to its chest. His lips move as he counts.
Leo (to Isla): Twenty-four beats. Write that down.
He sits the frog up against the baseboard, then the owl, then the lamb. All three lean in a row against the wall, facing the room.
Leo (to Isla): Nobody lies down in my hospital. Lying down makes you worse.
Leo checks the frog's chest once more, then the owl's, then the lamb's. Then he looks at your tote.
Leo (to Isla): The staff needs supplies. Nurse, what do we have?
Leo checks the frog's chest once more, then the owl's, then the lamb's. Then he looks at your tote.
Leo (to Isla): The staff needs supplies. Pretzels and cookies. Nurse, where are they?

stages.summary: Fetch the pretzel sticks and oat cookies from the kitchen and return to Leo in the playroom.

narrative_lines: Leo flips the chart over and smooths it flat on the rug. He pushes the red crayon back into your hand.
Leo (to Isla): Now the Warning Signs. On the back. Write that Owl has lines by his eyes when he comes home from work.
He holds up the frog and parts the fuzz beside its ear with one finger.
Leo (to Isla): And Frog has three white hairs right here. I counted them.
Leo (to Isla): Pop had a whole head of white hairs.

stages.summary: Choose a picture book from the book room, at the top of the house.
narrative_lines: Isla (to Leo): Doctor, the patients are getting restless. I think they need a story to settle them. I'll go and find one.
Leo (to Isla): Hm. Fine. Be fast.

stages.summary: Take the book back to Leo in the playroom.

narrative_lines: You take the folded oatmeal cloth from your tote and drape it over the toy shelf. You switch on the warm lamp by the beanbag and turn off the overhead light.
Leo climbs onto the window cushion and props the frog upright against his knee.
Leo (to Isla): One book. I'll monitor the frog.
On the first page, a small owl in an acorn helmet marches up and down an oak branch. Below him, a row of birds sleeps wing to wing along the bark.
Isla (to Leo): Little Owl marched up the branch. Little Owl marched down the branch. All night long, nobody fell.
Leo taps the acorn helmet in the picture.
Leo (to Isla): See, somebody has to stay awake. Because once you're asleep you can't tell if your branch is breaking.
You turn the page. The sky has gone gray, and the other birds lift their heads out of their feathers.
Isla (to Leo): Little Owl, said the birds, your eyes are drooping. Come and rest. We will watch the branch for you. But Little Owl only marched faster.
Leo slaps the page flat with his palm before you reach the end.
Leo (to Isla): BEEP BEEP! Nurse! Frog just swallowed a whole fire truck! His stomach is flashing red!
The siren fades, and Leo sits very still with the frog against his knee. He looks at Little Owl on the page for a long time.
Leo (to Isla): Isla. Grown-ups say "I'm just resting my eyes." When they're really tired.
Leo (to Isla): That's what Pop said. The day before the ambulance came.
Leo (to Isla): So when Mom lies down after work and says it, I drop my Lego bin. So she opens her eyes again.
The last page shows the old branch broken at the foot of the tree. The storm is over, and an old badger sits in the grass beside Little Owl.

Isla (to Leo): It was the storm, said Old Badger. The branch was old, and the storm was big. It was not the sleeping. Every night every bird sleeps, and every night every chest goes up and down, all by itself, until morning.
In the last picture, Little Owl tucks his head under his wing. Old Badger stays awake on the branch below.
Leo (to Isla): Badger's staying awake on the lower branch, though. And their chests keep going automatic.
Leo (to Isla): Is that how it is for real? Chests going automatic?
Leo reaches up to his coat zipper and unclips a tiny red plastic flashlight. He closes his fist around it and squeezes the middle with his thumb, and a small yellow beam falls on the frog's good eye.
Leo (to Isla): Pop got this for me at Miller's Hardware. Look. If you let go of the middle, the light goes right out.
He lets go, and the beam goes out. He squeezes it again.
Leo (to Isla): After everybody goes to bed, I stand in the hall by Mom and Dad's door. I squeeze it for two seconds. Just enough to see the blanket go up and down.
On the first page, a rabbit in a white coat stands behind a counter heaped with band-aids. In the waiting room, a line of animals holds up bandaged paws.
Isla (to Leo): Doctor Rabbit counted the band-aids. One for a sneeze. Two for a scratch. Three for a bump on the nose.
Leo leans over the page and counts the animals in the line.
Leo (to Isla): Rabbit's doing it wrong. You count the band-aids AFTER. Write that down.
On the last page, every animal leaves the clinic with a lollipop, and Doctor Rabbit hangs his white coat on a hook.
Isla (to Leo): And then Doctor Rabbit locked up the clinic and went home. The end.
Leo studies the picture of the empty waiting room.
Leo (to Isla): He didn't check anybody's chest. Not even once.
You open to the first page. An old gray bear sits down on a soft white cloud under a crescent moon.
Isla (to Leo): Old Bear was very old, and very, very tired. So he lay down on the cloud and went to sleep, and he never woke up.
Leo slaps the cover shut with both hands.
Leo (to Isla): That book is wrong. Sleeping isn't the same thing.
He pulls the frog into his lap and goes back to checking its pulse.
On the shelf, the little pear timer gives its soft five-minute click. Leo takes the plastic stethoscope off his neck and hangs it back on the toy shelf.
Leo (to Isla): Is that the five-minute? Rounds are almost over.

stages.summary: Sit on the back steps. Go through the kitchen and out the back.
narrative_lines: The timer on the shelf gives its single soft chime. Leo zips his red coat up to his chin and pulls a hat out of one sleeve.
Out in the waiting room, Gloria is already on her feet. Claire is standing just inside the front door, with her scrubs showing under her coat.
Claire (to Leo): Hey, bud. Mittens in your sleeves. Ready?
Leo (to Isla): Bye, Nurse. Same time next Tuesday. Bring the patients.
Back in the playroom, the chart is on the low table, with 24 BEATS across the top in red crayon. The frog, the owl and the lamb are still propped upright against the baseboard.
The front door clicks shut behind them, and the house settles into quiet.
The back steps are cold, and there is old snow along the fence. You set your tote beside you on the top step and sit down for five minutes before heading round to unchain your bike.
Inside your tote, your phone has buzzed.
